note: Machine-readable compatibility ledger: every compatibility scenario is tracked as pass / known-gap / not-applicable under a permanent hc-<suite>-<capability>-<case> id. Status, reason and recordedAt semantics follow ADR-0002 section 7; the ledger was established by T11 and absorbed the T09 known-gap records (tests/compat/types/expected-divergences.json).

entries.reason: T48 added Element.tagName/localName and the uppercased nodeName, but the four recorded attribute gaps remain. First, the prototype layout: MAD DOM owns the attribute methods on Node.prototype (the element's direct prototype), so getOwnPropertyDescriptor reports them present, while happy-dom inherits them from higher up the class chain (present: false) — the per-tag Element class hierarchy is tracked by T48A. Second, non-Element access: `text.getAttribute` reaches Core and throws the frozen HierarchyRequestError taxonomy, while happy-dom lacks the method on text nodes (TypeError "not a function") — also closed by T48A. Third, the napi4 error degradation: DOM-spec violations throw a plain Error carrying the frozen ERR_MAD_DOM_* code instead of a real DOMException with the happy-dom message, and fourth, Core validates the WHATWG Name production strictly (digit-led names rejected where happy-dom accepts them) — both tracked by T48B.

T48 kept the Node.textContent accessor matching happy-dom for every read/write, null-to-empty conversion, non-string coercion and deep-tree concatenation. Two gaps remain. First, the prototype layout: MAD DOM owns the accessor on Node.prototype (present: true with getter/setter on the element's direct prototype) while happy-dom inherits it from higher up the class chain (present: false) — the per-tag Element class hierarchy is tracked by T48A. Second, a NUL byte in the setter value: Core rejects it with ERR_MAD_DOM_INVALID_CHARACTER while happy-dom stores it verbatim — tracked by T48B.

T48 closed the document-readyState gap (now "interactive") and the Element.nodeName casing gap (HTML elements now report the uppercased tag, so the body snapshot's nodeName matches happy-dom byte for byte). The single remaining difference is the entry shape: mad-dom exports the extra createWindow() convenience while happy-dom's package entry does not, so `typeof entry.createWindow` reads "function" on mad-dom and "undefined" on happy-dom. Aligning the entry surface (making `new Window()` the documented construction path and retiring or masking the createWindow export) is tracked by the follow-up todo T48E; the scenario keeps recording the difference so the ledger stays honest until then.

T48 closed the Element.nodeName casing gap (HTML elements now report the uppercased tag, so the querySelectorAll list snapshot's nodeName fields match happy-dom). The single remaining difference is the entry shape: mad-dom exports the extra createWindow() convenience while happy-dom's package entry does not, so `typeof entry.createWindow` differs. Aligning the entry surface is tracked by the follow-up todo T48E; the scenario keeps recording the difference so the ledger stays honest until then.

T40 implements the first-batch form contract (value/name/disabled/checked/selected, form.elements, submit/reset and event order) but not the advanced constraint-validation machinery, and T48 records it as a known gap: MAD DOM's form.checkValidity()/reportValidity() always return true (no ValidityState, no constraint evaluation, no invalid event), while happy-dom evaluates the required/type constraints and exposes the per-control validation surface (validity / validationMessage / setCustomValidity / willValidate / checkValidity). Implementing the WHATWG constraint validation is tracked by the follow-up todo T48C.

The T42 registry (define/get/getName/whenDefined) and the synchronous lifecycle reactions match happy-dom, but three deliberate deviations remain. First, happy-dom's CustomElementRegistry.upgrade() is a documented no-op while MAD DOM performs a genuine spec-style upgrade (firing connectedCallback) — aligning the upgrade semantics is tracked by T48D. Second, `new DefinedClass()` mints a real detached element in happy-dom while MAD DOM's empty single-class base yields a bare object whose localName reads undefined — the per-tag Element class hierarchy is tracked by T48A. Third, the define-after-connect upgrade is in-place in MAD DOM while happy-dom physically replaces the element — also tracked by T48D.
